title: The Pied Piper of Hamelin
text:
The legend says that in 1284 the town of Hamelin in Lower Saxony was overrun by rats and mice. A stranger appeared in a coat of many colors and offered to rid the town of them for a fee. The townspeople agreed. He took out a pipe and began to play, and the rats came pouring out of every house and followed him to the river Weser, where they waded in and drowned.

With the rats gone, the townspeople refused to pay him. In Browning's poem the mayor offers fifty guilders instead of the agreed thousand and treats the piper as a joke. The piper left, angry.

On the feast of Saints John and Paul, June 26, he came back, dressed as a hunter, and played a different tune in the streets. This time the children came running out to follow him, a hundred and thirty of them according to the old account. He led them out of the town gate and into a mountain, and they were never seen again. In the Grimms' account, two children straggled back, one blind and one mute, and could tell only part of what happened. In Browning's poem, a lame boy was left behind.
lesson: A promise made under pressure must still be kept once the pressure is gone. Cheating someone who solved your problem is the surest way to create a worse one.
people: The piper, the mayor and council of Hamelin, the children of Hamelin
source: Brothers Grimm, Deutsche Sagen (1816); Robert Browning, The Pied Piper of Hamelin (1842)
caveat: Town records suggest some real loss of Hamelin's children in 1284, but the rat catching was added to the legend only in the 16th century.
